newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German panel calls for sharp cut in top tax rate.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German panel calls for sharp cut in top tax rate.

text.p: A government panel weighed into Germany's hot tax debate on Tuesday with a radical plan to impose a three-tier income tax system with a 30 percent top rate -- sharply below the current top rate of 53 percent.
The rate proposed by the independent advisors to the Economics Ministry for the top tax rate is below levels being toyed with by Bonn's centre-right coalition.
The advisors also called for lower taxation of companies and interest on savings, partly offset by scrapping many of Germany's myriad tax breaks.
"Everyone knows that there is no way around a fundamental reform of our tax system," panel chief Professor Manfred Neumann told a news conference.

All shades of political opinion agree Germany's tax system is complex, onerous and encourages evasion. Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition meets next month to map out a plan for a big tax reform which will probably take effect in 1999.

Revenue forecasts have just been cut by 10 billion marks ($6.69 billion) for 1997 despite increased recovery hopes. That shows the tax system is failing and adds to the risk of high budget deficits that threaten Germany's bid to join European monetary union in 1999, economists say.

Kohl's Christian Democrats want to cut top-rate income tax to 35 percent, while the entry rate should fall to 20 percent or below from 26 percent. Abolishing tax breaks would result in a net tax reduction of 20-30 billion marks.
But, while proposing a similar reduction in the overall tax burden, the government panel goes further in calling for cuts:
-- Income between 12,000 and 20,000 marks should be taxed at just 10 percent. The 20 percent rate should go from 20,000 to 30,000 marks. Extra income pays for the 30 percent top rate.
-- Taxes on company profits should fall to 30 percent.
-- Interest earnings should be taxed at 15 percent instead of the marginal income tax rate.
-- Share dividends should be tax-free to prevent double taxation of company profits.
-- "Like income should be treated alike", so benefits like unemployment pay should be liable to income tax in the same way as earned income.
-- Speculative profits should be taxed, but only as long as losses can be offset against tax.
Neumann said the plan would cut 102 billion marks in taxes. By scrapping 77 billion marks in tax breaks, it would ease the overall burden on taxpayers by around 25 billion marks.
He said it would help promote business, boost job creation and trigger the return of flight capital to Germany.

The tax system would also become fairer, simpler and more transparent. And it would also provide room to cut the state's share of total spending -- which at half of gross domestic product is well above competing European countries.
The panel's proposal, although only a discussion paper, was welcomed by Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt as vindicating the government's plans to reduce taxes.

"Germany has fallen behind in the race for internationally mobile capital," said Rexrodt, who is a member of the traditionally pro-business junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP). "A significant cut in income and corporation tax rates would be a vital signal."

But some of the ideas being proposed by the panel already look to be catching on. Finance Minister Theo Waigel told a tax conference at the weekend that making benefits liable to tax "made sense for the tax system".
